prompt: Classify the following five changes: (1) price level rises; (2) business confidence rises; (3) domestic currency appreciates because foreign investors suddenly prefer domestic assets; (4) price level falls; (5) government purchases rise. Which classification is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Only (2) and (5) affect AD; the other changes affect only supply.

options.label: B
options.text: All five changes shift AD.

options.label: C
options.text: (1) movement up/left along AD; (2) shift right; (3) shift left; (4) movement down/right along AD; (5) shift right.

options.label: D
options.text: (1) shift left; (2) movement right; (3) movement left; (4) shift right; (5) movement right.

options.label: E
options.text: (1) and (4) shift AD, while (2), (3), and (5) are movements along it.

explanation: The distinction depends on whether the price level causes the change; price-level changes produce movement along AD. Independent changes in confidence, exchange rates, or G alter spending components at every price level and shift AD.

prompt: An economy initially has AD1. Then household consumption rises by $70B, planned investment falls by $30B, government purchases rise by $20B, and net exports fall by $10B. At the same time, the price level falls from 115 to 105. Ignoring multiplier effects, which graphical description is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The autonomous component changes shift AD right by a net $50B; the price-level fall then causes movement down and right along the new AD2 curve.

options.label: B
options.text: The price-level fall shifts AD right by $10B and the component changes cause movement along AD1.

options.label: C
options.text: The net component change is zero, so only movement along AD1 occurs.

options.label: D
options.text: The combined changes cannot be separated conceptually because every price-level change shifts AD.

options.label: E
options.text: AD shifts left by $50B and the price-level fall moves up and left along AD2.

explanation: The autonomous spending change is +70 -30 +20 -10 = +$50B, so AD shifts right. Separately, a lower price level changes the quantity demanded along whichever AD curve is now in place, producing a movement down/right along AD2.
graphDescription: Vertical axis: Price Level. Horizontal axis: Real GDP. AD1 shifts right to AD2. A point at PL=115 on AD1 is compared with a lower-PL point at 105 on AD2; the task is to separate the shift from the movement along the new curve.

prompt: At a constant price level, the following autonomous spending changes occur: C +$90B, I -$55B, G -$20B, NX +$5B. What happens to AD before multiplier effects?

options.label: A
options.text: The direction cannot be determined without knowing the MPC.

options.label: B
options.text: AD is unchanged because C and I move in opposite directions.

options.label: C
options.text: AD increases by $170B and shifts right.

options.label: D
options.text: AD decreases by $20B and shifts left.

options.label: E
options.text: AD increases by $20B and shifts right.

explanation: Add the changes in the four AD components: +90 -55 -20 +5 = +$20B. The MPC determines multiplier size in Topic 3.2, but it is not needed to determine the initial direction of the Topic 3.1 AD shift.

prompt: A student argues: 'If the domestic currency appreciates, AD always shifts left.' Which evaluation is most precise?

options.label: A
options.text: The statement is always correct because exchange rates can never help explain AD's slope.

options.label: B
options.text: The statement is correct only when government spending is unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: The statement is always false because appreciation always raises net exports.

options.label: D
options.text: The statement is incomplete: an appreciation caused by a non-price factor shifts AD left through lower NX, but an appreciation that occurs as part of the price-level-induced exchange rate effect helps explain movement along a given AD curve.

options.label: E
options.text: The statement is false because exchange rates affect SRAS rather than AD.

explanation: Topic 3.1 uses the exchange rate in two logically different ways. An endogenous appreciation triggered by a price-level change is part of the slope mechanism; an exogenous appreciation changes NX at each price level and shifts AD.

prompt: A graph is drawn with Price Level on the vertical axis, Real GDP on the horizontal axis, and AD upward sloping. The student explains: 'Higher prices cause firms to produce more, so aggregate demand rises.' What is the best critique?

options.label: A
options.text: The curve should be vertical because real GDP demanded never responds to the price level.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the horizontal-axis label is wrong; AD should use nominal GDP.

options.label: C
options.text: The graph is correct because all macroeconomic curves slope upward.

options.label: D
options.text: The reasoning is correct, but the curve should be labeled LRAS.

options.label: E
options.text: The axes are appropriate, but the curve and reasoning are wrong: the statement describes a short-run aggregate supply mechanism, while AD should slope downward because higher prices reduce real wealth and raise interest rates and the exchange value of the currency.

explanation: The student has confused demand and supply. Higher output prices relative to sticky input costs can explain upward-sloping SRAS, whereas Topic 3.1 AD slopes downward through the three demand-side effects.
graphDescription: Student graph: Price Level vertical, Real GDP horizontal, an upward-sloping curve labeled AD. The task is to diagnose the conceptual error.

prompt: Country A and Country B are identical except that households in A hold much more fixed nominal financial wealth. The price level rises by the same percentage in both countries. Which statement is most consistent with the real wealth effect?

options.label: A
options.text: The price-level increase raises real wealth in both countries.

options.label: B
options.text: The real wealth effect may produce a larger absolute decline in consumption in Country A because more nominal wealth loses purchasing power, though the direction of movement along AD is the same in both countries.

options.label: C
options.text: Country B experiences the larger wealth effect because it has less wealth to lose.

options.label: D
options.text: Country A's AD curve must shift left while Country B only moves along AD.

options.label: E
options.text: Neither country is affected because nominal wealth is unchanged.

explanation: The real wealth effect concerns the purchasing power of nominal wealth. Both countries experience a decline in real wealth when the price level rises; a larger stock of nominal wealth can make the absolute consumption response larger, but the price-level change is still represented as movement along each country's AD curve.

prompt: Assume the nominal money supply is fixed. The price level increases, but business investment is unusually insensitive to interest rates while household durable-goods purchases are highly interest sensitive. What does the interest rate effect still predict?

options.label: A
options.text: Higher money demand raises interest rates; aggregate spending still falls because interest-sensitive household consumption declines even if investment responds only weakly.

options.label: B
options.text: The interest rate effect disappears completely unless investment is interest sensitive.

options.label: C
options.text: Higher interest rates raise durable-goods consumption, so AD becomes upward sloping.

options.label: D
options.text: The price level increase shifts AD left because the money supply is fixed.

options.label: E
options.text: Only net exports can respond to higher interest rates.

explanation: The interest rate effect works through any interest-sensitive component of spending, especially C and I. If one component responds weakly, the mechanism can still operate through the other.

prompt: A price-level increase raises domestic interest rates. Foreign investors respond strongly, but export demand is nearly insensitive to the exchange rate while import demand is very sensitive. Which conclusion is most consistent with the exchange rate effect?

options.label: A
options.text: AD shifts left rather than moving along AD because any NX change shifts the curve.

options.label: B
options.text: The exchange rate effect disappears unless both exports and imports respond equally.

options.label: C
options.text: The exchange rate effect changes SRAS, not aggregate demand.

options.label: D
options.text: Currency appreciation can still reduce net exports substantially because cheaper imports increase even if exports respond weakly.

options.label: E
options.text: Currency appreciation must increase net exports because imports are price sensitive.

explanation: An appreciation lowers NX if it reduces exports and/or raises imports. The exact strength of each channel can differ; what matters for the slope effect is that the price-level-induced appreciation lowers NX and the quantity of real GDP demanded.

prompt: An economy experiences two simultaneous events: consumer confidence collapses and the price level falls. Which statement is necessarily correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The confidence collapse shifts AD left, while the lower price level causes movement down and right along the new, left-shifted AD curve; the final quantity of real GDP demanded relative to the original point is ambiguous without magnitudes.

options.label: B
options.text: Both events shift AD in opposite directions, so the final AD curve is unchanged.

options.label: C
options.text: AD must shift left and the quantity demanded must fall because shifts always dominate movements.

options.label: D
options.text: Both events cause movements along AD, so the curve does not shift.

options.label: E
options.text: AD must shift right because the lower price level dominates all other effects.

explanation: The events operate through different mechanisms. Confidence is a non-price determinant of C and shifts AD left; the lower price level changes the quantity demanded along the new curve; without the sizes of the effects, the final quantity relative to the original point cannot be known.

prompt: An economy experiences an increase in government purchases at the same time the price level rises. Which representation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The G increase is movement along AD while the price-level rise shifts AD left.

options.label: B
options.text: The price-level rise prevents G from affecting aggregate demand.

options.label: C
options.text: G increases shift AD right to AD2; the higher price level then moves the economy up and left along AD2. Without magnitudes, the final real GDP demanded relative to the original point is ambiguous.

options.label: D
options.text: Both changes shift AD in opposite directions and therefore cancel exactly.

options.label: E
options.text: Both changes shift AD right.

explanation: A change in G is a shift determinant; a change in the price level is a movement-along-curve determinant. The direction of the final quantity relative to the starting point depends on the sizes of the rightward shift and the upward/left movement.
graphDescription: Vertical axis: Price Level. Horizontal axis: Real GDP. AD1 shifts right to AD2 because G rises. The relevant point on AD2 is at a higher price level than the original point on AD1.

prompt: A $100 billion increase in autonomous government purchases occurs. Which statement is most appropriate for Topic 3.1?

options.label: A
options.text: The increase causes only movement along AD because G is on the vertical axis.

options.label: B
options.text: AD shifts right by exactly $100 billion in equilibrium real GDP, regardless of the multiplier.

options.label: C
options.text: The increase in G shifts the AD curve to the right; Topic 3.1 identifies the direction of the shift, while Topic 3.2 is needed to quantify any multiplied change in total spending or output.

options.label: D
options.text: AD does not shift until the multiplier process is complete.

options.label: E
options.text: The increase shifts SRAS right because all government purchases raise productive capacity.

explanation: Topic 3.1 establishes that autonomous changes in G shift aggregate demand. The expenditure multiplier is a separate Topic 3.2 concept, so a 3.1 question should not equate the initial spending change with the eventual equilibrium output response.

prompt: Four economies experience the following autonomous changes at an unchanged price level. Which economy has the largest rightward AD shift before multiplier effects? Economy A: C +40, I +10, G 0, NX -5. Economy B: C +15, I +20, G +25, NX -10. Economy C: C +60, I -20, G -10, NX +5. Economy D: C +30, I +15, G +10, NX -20.

options.label: A
options.text: All four have the same shift because each contains four components.

options.label: B
options.text: Economy A, with a net increase of 45.

options.label: C
options.text: Economy D, with a net increase of 35.

options.label: D
options.text: Economy C, with a net increase of 35.

options.label: E
options.text: Economy B, with a net increase of 50.

explanation: Compute the net autonomous spending change: A = 40+10-5 = 45; B = 15+20+25-10 = 50; C = 60-20-10+5 = 35; D = 30+15+10-20 = 35. The largest rightward shift is therefore in Economy B.

prompt: A domestic price-level increase leads to currency appreciation through the exchange rate effect. At the same time, a separate political event abroad causes foreign consumers to strongly prefer domestic exports. Which statement is best?

options.label: A
options.text: The political event shifts SRAS right, while the price-level increase shifts AD left.

options.label: B
options.text: The price-level increase causes movement up/left along the current AD curve through the exchange rate effect, while the independent rise in foreign demand shifts AD right through higher NX; the final quantity demanded is ambiguous without magnitudes.

options.label: C
options.text: Both events shift AD right because exports rise.

options.label: D
options.text: Both events cause movement along the existing AD curve because they involve the exchange rate.

options.label: E
options.text: The two events must cancel because one lowers NX and the other raises it.

explanation: A price-level-induced trade response belongs to the slope of AD, whereas an independent change in foreign preferences changes exports at every price level and shifts AD. The two effects can operate simultaneously but need not offset exactly.

prompt: Suppose the domestic price level falls. Trace the complete exchange-rate channel, assuming the money supply is fixed and international capital is mobile.

options.label: A
options.text: Lower price level -> government spending rises -> interest rate falls -> NX rises.

options.label: B
options.text: Lower price level -> higher money demand -> higher interest rate -> capital inflow -> appreciation -> NX rises.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower price level -> currency depreciation directly -> LRAS shifts right -> output demanded rises.

options.label: D
options.text: Lower price level -> lower transactions demand for money -> lower domestic interest rate -> financial capital outflow -> currency depreciation -> exports rise and imports fall -> NX rises -> quantity of real GDP demanded rises.

options.label: E
options.text: Lower price level -> lower interest rate -> capital inflow -> appreciation -> NX falls -> quantity demanded rises.

explanation: This is the reverse of the price-level increase exchange-rate effect. The full chain reinforces the negative slope of AD: a lower price level ultimately raises NX and the quantity of domestic output demanded.

prompt: An increase in personal taxes reduces consumption by $40B, but stronger business expectations raise investment by $25B and higher foreign income raises net exports by $20B. Government purchases do not change. What happens to AD before multiplier effects?

options.label: A
options.text: AD shifts right by $85B because all absolute changes are added.

options.label: B
options.text: The direction cannot be determined without the price level.

options.label: C
options.text: AD remains unchanged because the number of positive and negative components is irrelevant.

options.label: D
options.text: AD shifts right by $5B because -40 +25 +20 = +5.

options.label: E
options.text: AD shifts left by $5B because taxes always dominate investment and exports.

explanation: The net change in the four AD components is -40 +25 +0 +20 = +$5B. The small positive total means planned aggregate spending is higher at each price level, so AD shifts right.

prompt: Which classification of six events is fully correct? (1) PL rises; (2) wealth rises because stock prices rise; (3) PL falls; (4) firms expect lower future profits; (5) foreign income rises; (6) domestic currency appreciates because of an exogenous financial-capital inflow.

options.label: B
options.text: Movements: (1) up/left and (3) down/right. Shifts: (2) right, (4) left, (5) right, (6) left.

options.label: C
options.text: All six are shifts because each changes spending.

options.label: D
options.text: Only (2) and (4) shift AD; foreign income and exchange rates affect supply.

explanation: Price-level changes move along AD. Independent changes in wealth, expectations, foreign income, and exchange rates alter C, I, or NX at each price level and therefore shift the curve.

prompt: A graph shows AD1 shifting right to AD2. After the shift, the price level rises and the economy moves from point B to point C on AD2. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The initial non-price increase in an AD component caused AD1 -> AD2; the subsequent price-level increase caused movement from B to C up and left along AD2.

options.label: B
options.text: The price-level increase caused the original AD1 -> AD2 shift, while the spending change caused movement along AD2.

options.label: C
options.text: The graph is impossible because a price-level change cannot occur after an AD shift.

options.label: D
options.text: Both changes are movements along the same AD curve.

options.label: E
options.text: Both changes are shifts, first right and then left.

explanation: This question separates curve shifts from movement along a curve. A non-price change in C, I, G, or NX changes the entire AD schedule; once the new curve exists, a price-level change selects a different point on that same curve.
graphDescription: Vertical axis: Price Level. Horizontal axis: Real GDP. AD1 shifts right to AD2. Point B lies on AD2 at a lower price level; point C lies above and left of B on AD2.

prompt: A comprehensive Topic 3.1 scenario: (a) identify what AD measures; (b) explain why it slopes downward; (c) determine what happens if firms independently raise investment at every price level. Which response is fully correct?

options.label: A
options.text: (a) AD measures nominal GDP; (b) scarcity explains the slope; (c) investment has no effect on AD.

options.label: B
options.text: (a) AD relates interest rates to investment; (b) sticky wages explain the slope; (c) investment raises SRAS only.

options.label: C
options.text: (a) AD is vertical at Yf; (b) flexible prices explain the slope; (c) investment shifts LRAS only.

options.label: D
options.text: (a) AD relates a single good's price to quantity; (b) income and substitution effects explain the slope; (c) investment causes movement along AD.

options.label: E
options.text: (a) AD relates the price level to real GDP demanded by C, I, G, and NX; (b) the real wealth, interest rate, and exchange rate effects explain the negative slope; (c) higher autonomous investment shifts AD right.

explanation: The correct response synthesizes MOD-2.A.1, A.2, and A.3 without importing mechanisms from SRAS, LRAS, or microeconomic demand.

prompt: Two students debate the slope of AD. Student 1 says: 'A higher price level lowers real wealth, which reduces C.' Student 2 says: 'A higher price level raises money demand and interest rates, which reduces C and I, and it can appreciate the currency, reducing NX.' Who is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Only Student 2 is correct; real wealth does not affect consumption.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither is correct; AD slopes down because of income and substitution effects for a single good.

options.label: C
options.text: Both are incorrect because the price level shifts AD rather than causing movement along it.

options.label: D
options.text: Only Student 1 is correct; interest rates and exchange rates are shift factors only.

options.label: E
options.text: Both students are correct; together they describe the real wealth, interest rate, and exchange rate effects.

explanation: Student 1 describes the real wealth effect. Student 2 describes the interest rate effect and the exchange rate effect; these are precisely the three mechanisms identified in MOD-2.A.2.

prompt: A student submits an AD graph with the following errors: horizontal axis labeled Nominal GDP; curve labeled D; and a rightward shift attributed to a fall in the price level. Which correction set is complete?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep the labels but redraw AD upward sloping.

options.label: B
options.text: Only relabel the curve AD; the other elements are correct.

options.label: C
options.text: Relabel the horizontal axis Quantity and show the price-level fall as a leftward shift.

options.label: D
options.text: Relabel the horizontal axis Real GDP, label the curve AD, and show a price-level fall as movement down/right along the existing AD curve rather than a rightward shift.

options.label: E
options.text: Relabel the vertical axis Interest Rate and keep Nominal GDP on the horizontal axis.

explanation: Skill 4.A requires accurate labels and graphical representation. Aggregate demand uses Real GDP horizontally, must be identified as AD, and price-level changes produce movement along the curve.
graphDescription: Student graph: vertical axis Price Level; horizontal axis Nominal GDP; downward curve labeled D; second curve shifted right with note 'Price level falls.'

prompt: The price level rises by 8 percent while the nominal money supply is unchanged. Which statement is most consistent with the interest rate effect, without making an unsupported numerical claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The nominal money supply automatically rises by 8 percent, leaving interest rates unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: AD shifts left by exactly 8 percent because the price level is 8 percent higher.

options.label: C
options.text: The transactions demand for money rises, putting upward pressure on interest rates and downward pressure on interest-sensitive C and I, so the quantity of real GDP demanded falls.

options.label: D
options.text: Interest rates must rise by exactly 8 percent, so investment falls by exactly 8 percent.

options.label: E
options.text: Interest rates fall because real money balances rise.

explanation: The CED specifies the direction of the interest-rate-effect chain, not a one-for-one numerical relationship. A higher price level raises transactions demand for money and tends to raise interest rates, lowering interest-sensitive spending.

prompt: An economy experiences a lower price level and a simultaneous exogenous appreciation of its currency. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The appreciation affects only SRAS, so the quantity demanded must rise.

options.label: B
options.text: Both events increase net exports, so AD must shift right.

options.label: C
options.text: The lower price level shifts AD right and the appreciation moves up AD.

options.label: D
options.text: The lower price level creates movement down/right along AD through the slope effects, while the exogenous appreciation reduces NX and shifts AD left; the final real GDP demanded is ambiguous without magnitudes.

options.label: E
options.text: Both events cause movement down/right along the same AD curve.

explanation: The price-level change and the independent exchange-rate change must be represented separately. One is movement along AD; the other changes NX at each price level and shifts the curve.

prompt: A policymaker says: 'Because a decrease in the price level increases consumption, investment, and net exports, the AD curve shifts right whenever the price level falls.' What is the best response?

options.label: A
options.text: The policymaker is correct only if government purchases also rise.

options.label: B
options.text: The policymaker is correct; any increase in C, I, or NX must shift AD right regardless of its cause.

options.label: C
options.text: The spending responses are real, but the conclusion is wrong: because the price level caused them, they explain movement down/right along the existing AD curve, not a shift of the curve.

options.label: D
options.text: The policymaker is wrong because price-level changes affect only SRAS.

options.label: E
options.text: The policymaker is wrong because a lower price level reduces all three components.

explanation: A key Topic 3.1 distinction is cause, not merely which component changes. C, I, and NX can change as endogenous responses to the price level; those changes form the slope of AD; only non-price-level changes in components shift AD.

prompt: A graph shows AD1. Then consumption falls by $30B and investment falls by $20B, shifting AD to AD2. Afterward the price level falls enough that the quantity of real GDP demanded on AD2 rises by an amount larger than the original leftward shift. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: AD2 remains to the left of AD1, even though the final quantity demanded can exceed the original quantity because movement along AD2 can be large enough to offset the shift at the observed price levels.

options.label: B
options.text: Such an outcome is impossible because a leftward shift always lowers quantity demanded at every possible price level relative to every point on AD1.

options.label: C
options.text: The leftward shift disappears once the price level falls.

options.label: D
options.text: A price-level fall shifts AD2 back to AD1.

options.label: E
options.text: AD2 must cross to the right of AD1 if final quantity demanded exceeds the original quantity.

explanation: A leftward shift means that at any given price level, AD2 demands less real GDP than AD1. It does not mean every point on AD2 has less quantity than every point on AD1; comparing points at different price levels mixes a curve shift with movement along the curve.
graphDescription: Vertical axis: Price Level. Horizontal axis: Real GDP. AD2 lies left of AD1. An original point A is high on AD1; a final point C is much lower on AD2 and can lie to the right of A in terms of Real GDP because the price level is substantially lower.

prompt: Country Zeta reports the following at unchanged price level: household consumption +$45B, residential investment +$15B, federal transfer payments +$20B, federal purchases +$10B, exports -$5B, imports +$10B. If the transfer increase raises consumption by an additional $12B, what is the initial net change in AD before multiplier effects?
explanation: Count only changes in AD components, while including the transfer's indirect effect on C: C = +45 +12 = +57; I = +15; G = +10; NX changes by exports -5 and imports +10, so NX = -15. Net AD change = 57 +15 +10 -15 = +$67B; the $20B transfer itself is not directly part of G.

prompt: A complete graphing task asks a student to show an autonomous decrease in net exports followed by a fall in the price level. Which construction is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: First move down AD1; then shift SRAS left.

options.label: B
options.text: First shift AD1 right; then move up AD2.

options.label: C
options.text: Shift AD1 left twice, once for NX and once for the lower price level.

options.label: D
options.text: Show only a movement down AD1 because net exports are part of the exchange rate effect.

options.label: E
options.text: First shift AD1 left to AD2; then show a movement down and right along AD2 to a lower price level and higher quantity of real GDP demanded than at the initial point on AD2.

explanation: An autonomous NX decrease changes aggregate demand at every price level and shifts the curve left. A subsequent price-level fall is represented by movement along the new curve, down and to the right.
graphDescription: Vertical axis: Price Level. Horizontal axis: Real GDP. AD1 shifts left to AD2 because NX falls. On AD2, a point at higher PL moves downward/right to a second point as PL falls.

prompt: Which statement most accurately evaluates this claim: 'Whenever consumption changes, the AD curve must shift.'?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is false because consumption is not part of aggregate demand.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is true only when investment changes at the same time.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is true because C is always a shift variable.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is false because only government purchases and net exports can shift AD.

options.label: E
options.text: The claim is false because consumption can change either as an endogenous response to a price-level change, which contributes to movement along AD, or because of a non-price determinant, which shifts AD.

explanation: Topic 3.1 distinguishes endogenous component responses to the price level from autonomous component changes. The former explain the curve's slope; the latter shift the curve.

prompt: Which response correctly integrates all three essential-knowledge statements of Topic 3.1 using one example?

options.label: A
options.text: AD equals potential GDP; higher prices leave quantity demanded unchanged; higher G moves along AD.

options.label: B
options.text: At each price level AD totals C+I+G+NX; a rise in the price level lowers the quantity demanded through real wealth, interest rate, and exchange rate effects; an independent rise in G then shifts the entire AD curve right.

options.label: C
options.text: AD totals C+S+T+M; higher prices raise quantity demanded through sticky wages; higher G shifts SRAS right.

options.label: D
options.text: AD totals only C and I; higher prices reduce quantity demanded only through real wealth; higher G shifts LRAS.

options.label: E
options.text: AD totals C+I+G+NX; higher prices shift AD left; higher G then moves down the shifted curve.

explanation: The correct response states the definition/components from MOD-2.A.1, the three slope effects from MOD-2.A.2, and the non-price component shift rule from MOD-2.A.3.
